response.title: How many solar panels do I need to keep a power station charged in winter when it's cloudy most days?
response.answer:
If it's cloudy most days in winter, you'll typically need 2–5 times more solar panel capacity than you would in summer to keep a portable power station charged.

The exact number depends on how much electricity you use daily, not just the battery size.

How many panels do you need?

Assuming 200W solar panels, winter conditions with frequent clouds, and approximately 0.5–1.5 equivalent full-sun hours per day:

These estimates include roughly 20% charging losses. Very dark, rainy days may produce substantially less power.

One important consideration: solar panels cannot guarantee a full battery every day during prolonged cloudy weather. You'll also want enough battery capacity to cover 2–4 days of consumption without meaningful charging.

Three questions to size your system accurately

Which power station do you have? For example, EcoFlow DELTA 2, Jackery Explorer 1000, or Anker SOLIX F2000.

What will you power? A refrigerator, laptop, lights, heater, or something else?

Where are you located? City or ZIP code is enough to estimate winter solar production.

With those details, I can calculate how many 200W or 400W panels you need, including how to handle several consecutive cloudy days.
markup:
If it's cloudy most days in winter, you'll typically need **2–5 times more solar panel capacity** than you would in summer to keep a portable power station charged.

The exact number depends on how much electricity you use daily, not just the battery size.

## How many panels do you need?

Assuming 200W solar panels, winter conditions with frequent clouds, and approximately 0.5–1.5 equivalent full-sun hours per day:

| Daily electricity use | 200W panels needed |
|---|---|
| 200 Wh | 1–3 panels |
| 500 Wh | 2–6 panels |
| 1,000 Wh (1 kWh) | 4–12 panels |
| 2,000 Wh (2 kWh) | 8–24 panels |

These estimates include roughly 20% charging losses. Very dark, rainy days may produce substantially less power.

## What cloudy weather does to solar output

<box gap={2}>
  {#each [{name:"Clear winter day",p:100},{name:"Partly cloudy",p:55},{name:"Overcast",p:20},{name:"Heavy clouds / rain",p:5}] as x}
    <row align="center" gap={3}>
      <box width="145px">
        <text size="xs">{x.name}</text>
      </box>
      <box flex="1" background="surface-tertiary" height="12px" radius="sm" clip>
        <box background={x.p>=55?"#D5A044":x.p>=20?"#7994A6":"#9CA3AF"} width={`${x.p}%`} height="100%" radius="sm"/>
      </box>
      <box width="42px">
        <text size="xs" tabularNums textAlign="end">{x.p}%</text>
      </box>
    </row>
  {/each}
  <caption>Illustrative instantaneous output relative to rated panel power, not guaranteed daily production.</caption>
</box>

A 200W panel might generate 800–1,000 Wh on a good sunny day, but only 100–300 Wh over a cloudy winter day, and even less during prolonged storms.

## Calculate your own setup

{@body const [daily,setDaily] = DIL.useState(500)}
{@body const [panel,setPanel] = DIL.useState("200")}
{@body const [sun,setSun] = DIL.useState("1")}
{@body const count = Math.ceil(daily/(Number(panel)*Number(sun)*0.8))}
<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <text weight="medium">Daily electricity consumption</text>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    <text color="secondary" size="sm">Energy used per day</text>
    <title size="lg" color="default" tabularNums>{daily.toLocaleString()} Wh</title>
  </row>
  <slider min={100} max={3000} step={100} value={daily} onChange={setDaily}/>
  <text weight="medium">Panel wattage</text>
  <radio-group value={panel} onChange={setPanel} direction="row">
    <radio value="100">100W</radio>
    <radio value="200">200W</radio>
    <radio value="400">400W</radio>
  </radio-group>
  <text weight="medium">Average equivalent full-sun hours in winter</text>
  <radio-group direction="col" value={sun} onChange={setSun}>
    <radio value="0.5">0.5 hours — very cloudy</radio>
    <radio value="1">1 hour — mostly cloudy</radio>
    <radio value="2">2 hours — mixed conditions</radio>
    <radio value="3">3 hours — relatively sunny</radio>
  </radio-group>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" padding={3} gap={1}>
    <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="sm">Estimated solar panels required</text>
    <row align="baseline" gap={2}>
      <title size="2xl" color="default" tabularNums>{count}</title>
      <text>× {panel}W panels</text>
    </row>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Total rated solar capacity: {(count*Number(panel)).toLocaleString()}W. Based on average daily energy balance and 80% system efficiency; not a guarantee during consecutive dark days.</text>
  </box>
</box>

One important consideration: **solar panels cannot guarantee a full battery every day during prolonged cloudy weather.** You'll also want enough battery capacity to cover 2–4 days of consumption without meaningful charging.

## Three questions to size your system accurately

1. **Which power station do you have?** For example, EcoFlow DELTA 2, Jackery Explorer 1000, or Anker SOLIX F2000.
2. **What will you power?** A refrigerator, laptop, lights, heater, or something else?
3. **Where are you located?** City or ZIP code is enough to estimate winter solar production.

With those details, I can calculate how many 200W or 400W panels you need, including how to handle several consecutive cloudy days.
